name: Ruins of Ilun
desc: A silent monastery world, carved by the First Builders. The stones hum at night.

gm.feel: Cold stone, lamp oil and the smell of bread baked once a week for far too few people. The halls were cut for bodies taller than anyone alive, so every doorway makes you feel like a child, and at dusk the walls begin a hum you feel in your teeth before you hear it. Nothing is sold here: the monks take payment in silence, which means sitting with them until you've stopped wanting what you came for or you're sure you still do.

districts.name: The Listening Hall
districts.desc: A long nave with no roof, where the last monks sit on worn stone in shifts, and have done for a thousand years without a break. Nobody speaks above a whisper here, and the echoes come back late.

districts.name: The Empty Cells
districts.desc: Hundreds of novice cells, nearly all of them vacant now, each with a name painted over the door. Brother Cael still sweeps them every week.

districts.name: The Under-Stair
districts.desc: A First Builder stairway going down further than anyone has walked. The steps are the wrong height for every people that has ever lived, and far below the last lamp the walls are cut with long lists of names.

districts.name: The Wind Gardens
districts.desc: Terraces of grey lichen and bitter herbs on the cliff face, tended by the very old. It's the only place in the monastery where anyone laughs.

complications: A Hegemony Inquisitor's ship has entered orbit, and has politely requested permission to land.
Your people's boots and voices have broken a silence that's lasted three hundred years, and an old monk has simply stopped eating in protest.
The hum stops. It has never done that, and every monk in the hall opens their eyes at once.
A Resonant on your crew starts to answer the stones in their sleep, and they don't remember doing it.
A band of Orrin heretics has come to the gates to debate the Abbess, and they don't intend to leave quietly.
Storms close the landing field for two days, leaving your party on a world where the food runs short.
secrets: Abbess Ione bought the Navy's rotation tables from Mother Quill six years before the Fall, through a lay brother who cooked here, paying in carved stone from an old crypt. She sang them through the stones to the Choir, because a long war would have killed everyone for nothing and a short one kept them. If she's asked plainly, she'll say yes, and she'd like her sums checked.

Nine monasteries of the Order stand empty, with the beds made and the doors opened from inside. During the Fall the monks got up in the same hour and walked out to meet the silver, under orders. Far down the Under-Stair, relief crews are carved on the walls by the century, up to 1,006 years ago, and then there's nothing.

The Ilun Codex has pages neatly cut from it, and a later hand has changed the word "sing" to "listen" in a dozen places. The first line of the Founding Rule has been chiselled off every copy. The Abbess has hidden the Codex where only someone listening for it could find it, and the hum it answers to is slowing by a tiny amount each year.

encounters: Abbess Ione meets you at the top of the stairs and answers the question you hadn't asked yet. Then she asks you, gently, why you came all this way to ask a different one.

Brother Cael is sweeping an empty cell and talking to the novice whose name is over the door. He flushes in rolling patterns of color when you find him, and asks whether you've ever met anyone from his year, anywhere, at all.
An ancient monk has broken six decades of silence to say one sentence to you, and he has to say it now: it's the location of a lost novice, and he'd rather you didn't tell the Abbess he knows.

A monk in the bakery has one sack of flour and a grudging interest in your crew. She'll bake for your landing party if someone can fix the oven's flue, and she'll want to know exactly why they want to help.

One of your crew who was raised here has come back to see their mother's name over a cell door. They want to take the stone home with them. The monks won't stop them, and they won't help, and they won't forgive it.
A novice of about fifteen, too young to be this calm, tells you she knows she'll die on the Under-Stair and asks if you'd like to see it first. She seems to be offering a tour.
Two old monks in the Wind Gardens are arguing in sign language about whether the hum has changed. One of them turns to you and signs, slowly so you can follow, asking which of them you agree with.

A Hegemony pilgrim's permit has somehow been stamped for tomorrow, and the woman holding it is a very devout middle-aged clerk from Vantor. She says she's only here to pray. She's got a small dampener hidden in her lunch tin, and she doesn't know what it does.

At dusk, as the hum begins, a member of your crew starts to weep and can't stop. The monks gather without a word to sit with them. It might take all night, and your ship's window closes in three hours.
You're shown the Long Bench, where every visitor since the founding has carved a question. Near the end, in fresh cuts, someone has carved a question in your own handwriting.

A monk who was once a fleet gunner offers to break his vows and come with you. He knows the Order's old signal codes, and he's the one who gets up at night to light the dead novices' lamps. If he leaves, nobody else will.

A heretic from Saint Orrin's Comet has been sitting outside the gates for forty days, burned on both hands. She's not asking to come in, only for someone to carry in a letter to the Abbess that says three words.

An old kitchen monk remembers a lay brother called Hob, the best cook the monastery ever had, who went off on a long market trip once, with a sack of carved stones out of the old crypt. He came back with something in an envelope, and died within the year. She'd like to know why you're asking, and she goes on kneading while you decide.

A very old Thessan pilgrim, who has been coming here every thirty years, wants to compare today's hum against the record in his head. He'd like to borrow your ship's sensors. What he finds makes him stop talking for the rest of your visit.
rumors: Don't sleep with your ear against the wall. My aunt did that on her pilgrimage, and now she keeps setting an extra place for dinner.
The Abbess knows everything about the First Builders, and she won't say any of it. I'd love to think that's wisdom, and not that she's scared.
Those stairs at the back go all the way down to the planet's core, and there's a door at the bottom. So I'm told by people who've never gone down them.
Every Order novice in the fleet says the same thing: the hum's the same note, in every monastery, for a thousand years. Then they stop talking and look at their feet.
They say the Hegemony's already got someone inside the monastery. If it were me, I'd have sent someone years ago, someone patient, and they'd be a very good monk by now.
Abbess Ione's a hundred and sixty years old, kept alive by Resonance. I don't care what the records say. Have you seen how she goes up those stairs?

My cousin ran supplies to the Order's priory on Seld. He got there after the Fall, and it was all perfectly tidy. The beds were made, and the doors were standing open. Nobody had broken a thing. You'd think somebody would have broken something.
The young one with the flickering skin, Brother Cael, he's the only one who'll chat. If you need to know something, ask him, and watch his arms when he answers. He can't help it.
The stones hum louder when someone's about to die on the world. My granddad worked the supply runs here, and they'd have the coffin measured before the fever started.
You can't buy anything on Ilun. You can sit with them for a while, and when you're leaving someone gives you a bag of bitter herbs. It works on stomach trouble, and it means they like you.
I heard that the monks here have been listening for a thousand years, and that they never told a soul what they were listening for. So what kind of person hears that, and goes to ask?
Those Orrin people say the monks have had the whole thing backward from day one. They would say that, they're out on a comet setting fire to themselves, but they're not stupid, is what I'm saying.
A freighter pilot told me she flew over the monastery at night with every system shut down, and her ship's hull was humming along. The note stayed with her for a week, and when it left she missed it.
There's a Choir Hunter that lands here, I swear. Lands, stands in the courtyard for an hour with its head on one side, and takes off again. Nobody will talk about it, and nobody will fire on it.
